A church that insists on young-earth creationism, that pretends the Bible has no contradictions, that refuses to engage with legitimate historical and scientific questions, is a church that has disqualified itself in the eyes of anyone with an internet connection and a willingness to read. The nones do not need the church to abandon its convictions. They need the church to hold its convictions honestly, acknowledging complexity, engaging counterarguments, and trusting that truth does not need to be protected from scrutiny.

The third is justice. The nones are, as a group, strongly committed to racial justice, economic equality, LGBTQ inclusion, and environmental stewardship. They are not looking for a church that adopts progressive positions as a marketing strategy. They are looking for a community that takes the prophetic tradition seriously, that reads Amos and Isaiah and the Sermon on the Mount and actually does what they say. The Black church tradition, which has always understood faith and justice as inseparable, offers a model that the broader church has largely failed to learn from.

The fourth is space for doubt. The nones have been burned by communities that demanded certainty and punished questions. They are looking for a tradition robust enough to contain doubt, a faith that does not shatter when tested. The ancient practice of lament, the honest prayer of a person who does not understand what God is doing and refuses to pretend otherwise, is precisely the spiritual resource the nones need. But most churches have eliminated lament from their worship, replacing it with an unrelenting optimism that feels dishonest to anyone who has suffered.

The fifth, and perhaps most fundamental, is genuine community. Not the superficial friendliness of a church lobby, where strangers shake hands and exchange pleasantries before retreating to their separate lives. Not the programmatic community of small groups organized by demographic category and guided by packaged curricula. But the deep, costly, vulnerable community that the New Testament describes: a body in which every member is known and needed, in which burdens are shared and sorrows are borne together, in which the weak are not discarded and the strong are not idolized.

> The rise of the nones is not, fundamentally, a story about the decline of faith. It is a story about the decline of institutions that have failed to embody what they claim to believe. The hunger for God, for meaning, for community, for justice, for transcendence has not diminished. What has diminished is the church's credibility as the place where those hungers can be fed.

This is not a counsel of despair. It is, if the church can hear it, a counsel of hope. The nones are not enemies of faith. They are, in many cases, seekers of faith who have been failed by the institutions that promised to nurture it. They have not stopped asking the deepest human questions: Why am I here? What is the meaning of suffering? How should I live? Is there something beyond this material existence that gives it all significance? They have merely stopped expecting the church to provide honest answers.

The path forward is not to develop better strategies for attracting the nones. It is to become the kind of community that does not need a strategy because its life together is its argument. A community that tells the truth. A community that does justice. A community that makes space for doubt and mystery. A community that worships a God who is not threatened by honest questions. A community that looks, in short, more like the one Jesus described and less like the ones we have built in his name.

The nones are watching. Some of them are waiting. Whether the church has the courage to become what it claims to be will determine whether they ever come through the door, not because they were marketed to, argued with, or guilted into returning, but because they saw something real and recognized it as the thing they had been looking for all along.

chapters.title: Why People Are Leaving the Church
chapters.summary: The exodus from organized Christianity is the defining religious story of our era. The reasons people leave are not the reasons most pastors assume, and what the departed still hunger for should unsettle every congregation that thinks the problem is better marketing.
chapters.body:
The numbers are no longer debatable. They have not been debatable for at least a decade, though the institutional church has spent much of that decade debating them anyway, as if the appropriate response to a hemorrhaging wound is a prolonged discussion about whether the patient is actually bleeding.

In 2006, Gallup found that 73 percent of Americans identified as Christian. By 2022, that number had fallen to 68 percent. Pew Research Center's 2021 data showed a steeper picture: only 63 percent of American adults identified as Christian, down from 78 percent in 2007. The Public Religion Research Institute placed the figure even lower, at 61 percent, in its 2023 American Values Atlas. These are not marginal fluctuations within the noise of survey methodology. These represent the most rapid secularization of any major Western nation in the modern era, compressed into roughly fifteen years.

But the headline numbers, as dramatic as they are, obscure what is actually happening. Christianity is not declining uniformly. Evangelical Protestantism has held relatively steady in raw numbers, though its share of the population is shrinking. Black Protestantism has remained stable. It is mainline Protestantism and, increasingly, Roman Catholicism that are experiencing catastrophic losses. The Catholic Church in the United States has lost roughly one-third of its cradle Catholics, a departure that would constitute a demographic emergency in any other institution. Former Catholics now represent the second-largest "denomination" in the country, outnumbered only by current Catholics.

The question that matters, of course, is not merely what the numbers say but why the numbers say it. And here the church has largely failed, not because it has not asked the question, but because it has consistently preferred comforting answers to honest ones.

## The Reasons Pastors Assume (And Why They Are Mostly Wrong)

Ask a typical pastor why people are leaving the church, and you will hear a predictable set of explanations. People are too busy. The culture has become too secular. Young people are distracted by technology. Sunday sports leagues compete with worship services. People are selfish, individualistic, consumerist. They want comfort, not commitment. They have been led astray by a hostile media.

These explanations share a common feature: they locate the problem entirely outside the church. The institution is fine. The product is excellent. The customers are defective. This is, to borrow a phrase from the business world, a catastrophically bad diagnosis, the kind that precedes bankruptcy.

The data tell a different story. When researchers actually ask people why they left, the answers are remarkably consistent across multiple studies, and they point the finger squarely at the institution itself.

Josh Packard and Ashleigh Hope's research, published in *Church Refugees* (2015), found that the people leaving churches were not the nominally committed or the spiritually indifferent. They were, disproportionately, the most involved members: Sunday school teachers, worship leaders, committee chairs, small group facilitators. These were not people who drifted away out of apathy. They were people who had given years, sometimes decades, of committed service and finally concluded that the institution was no longer worthy of their investment.

The Barna Group's extensive research, spanning two decades, has identified five primary drivers of church departure: hypocrisy (perceived disconnect between what the church preaches and how it behaves), political entanglement (the sense that the church has become an arm of a political party), intellectual dishonesty (the refusal to engage honestly with science, history, or difficult questions), exclusion (the treatment of women, LGBTQ individuals, racial minorities, or doubters as second-class members), and clergy abuse and cover-ups (the institutional protection of predators at the expense of victims).

Notice what is absent from this list. Nobody is leaving because worship services need better lighting. Nobody is leaving because the church lacks a coffee bar in the lobby. Nobody is leaving because the sermons are not entertaining enough. The fixation on stylistic upgrades that has consumed American church culture for the past three decades, the millions spent on fog machines and branded sermon series and Instagram-worthy lobbies, has been an elaborate exercise in treating a symptom that does not exist while ignoring the disease that does.

## Hypocrisy: The Original Sin of Institutional Religion

When leavers cite hypocrisy, they are not merely observing that Christians sometimes fail to live up to their ideals. Everyone understands that human beings are imperfect. What they are identifying is something more specific and more damaging: the systematic gap between the church's public moral pronouncements and its institutional behavior.

A church that preaches radical generosity while its senior pastor lives in a mansion funded by tithes from working-class families. A denomination that thunders against sexual immorality while quietly reassigning priests credibly accused of molesting children. A congregation that proclaims the equality of all people before God while maintaining an all-white, all-male leadership structure in a diverse community. These are not instances of individual moral failure. They are patterns of institutional dishonesty, and the people who leave can see them with a clarity that those inside the institution often cannot.

The sociologist Robert Wuthnow documented this dynamic extensively in his research on American religion. He found that institutional trust, once lost, is almost impossible to recover, and that the perception of hypocrisy is the single most corrosive force in religious disaffiliation. People can forgive failure. They cannot forgive pretense.

## The Political Captivity of the Church

The entanglement of American Christianity with partisan politics, particularly the near-total identification of white evangelicalism with the Republican Party, has driven more people from the church than any theological dispute in modern memory. This is not a partisan observation. It is a demographic fact.

Ryan Burge, a political scientist at Eastern Illinois University and a Baptist pastor, has documented this extensively. His data show that political identity now predicts religious affiliation more reliably than religious affiliation predicts political identity. In other words, people are not joining the Republican Party because they are evangelical. They are leaving evangelicalism because they are not Republican. The causal arrow has reversed.

For younger Americans especially, the association between Christianity and conservative politics has become so tight that many cannot imagine one without the other. A 2022 survey by the Survey Center on American Life found that among Americans under thirty who left their childhood religion, 60 percent cited the church's stance on social and political issues as a significant factor. When a twenty-five-year-old says, "I am not a Christian," she may not be making a theological statement about the divinity of Jesus. She may be making a sociological statement: "I do not belong to the political tribe that has claimed Christianity as its brand."

The tragedy of this is difficult to overstate. A faith tradition that began with an itinerant rabbi executed by the state has become, in the public imagination, a chaplaincy for state power. The cross, which was Rome's instrument of political terror, now appears on the podiums of political rallies. Whether or not individual churches endorse specific candidates, the brand contamination is real, and it is driving a generation away.

## What "Leaving" Actually Looks Like

The popular assumption, shared by both anxious churchgoers and triumphant secularists, is that people who leave the church become atheists. They do not. The data on this are unambiguous.

According to Pew Research Center's 2021 study, the fastest-growing religious category in America is not atheism or agnosticism but "nothing in particular," a category that now represents 20 percent of the adult population, up from 12 percent in 2007. This group is distinct from atheists and agnostics in important ways. Many of them believe in God or a higher power. Many pray, at least occasionally. Many describe themselves as spiritual. What they have rejected is not the sacred but the institution. They have not abandoned transcendence. They have abandoned organized religion.

The term that has emerged to describe this population is "spiritual but not religious," or SBNR. It is a clumsy phrase, and it frustrates theologians on both sides: traditional believers think it is shallow, and committed atheists think it is incoherent. But it describes something real. There are tens of millions of Americans who believe that the universe has a spiritual dimension, who seek meaning and connection beyond the material, who may even consider themselves followers of Jesus in some sense, but who have concluded that the institutional church is not the place where these needs can be met. They are not rejecting God. They are rejecting the church's claim to be God's authorized representative.

This distinction, between leaving God and leaving the institution, is one that the church has been catastrophically slow to understand. When a pastor says, "Young people are turning away from God," he is usually wrong. What young people are turning away from is the pastor's institution. The conflation of the two is itself part of the problem. An organization that cannot distinguish between itself and the divine has already lost the capacity for self-criticism that might save it.

## What the Leavers Say

In qualitative research, the voices of those who have left are remarkably consistent, and remarkably painful to hear.

> "I didn't leave because I stopped believing. I left because I couldn't keep pretending that what was happening in that building on Sunday morning had anything to do with Jesus." This sentiment, expressed with minor variations by hundreds of respondents in Packard and Hope's research, represents the dominant narrative of church departure.

David Kinnaman's research for the Barna Group, published in *You Lost Me* (2011) and *UnChristian* (2007), found that young adults who left the church described it as "overprotective" (stifling honest inquiry and engagement with the broader culture), "shallow" (failing to offer intellectually serious engagement with faith and doubt), "anti-science" (requiring rejection of established scientific consensus as a condition of belonging), "repressive" (particularly regarding sexuality, in ways perceived as harmful rather than holy), "exclusive" (unwelcoming to those who do not conform to narrow cultural norms), and "doubtless" (demanding certainty and punishing questions).

The theologian Sarah Bessey, who has written extensively about her own experience of church departure and return, describes what many leavers feel: "The church broke my heart long before the world ever could." This is not the language of indifference. It is the language of betrayal. People do not grieve institutions they never loved.

What makes these testimonies so devastating for the church is that they come disproportionately from people who were deeply invested. These are not outsiders lobbing criticism from a comfortable distance. These are people who sang in the choir, served on the building committee, led vacation Bible school, tithed faithfully, and wept during worship. They left not because they did not care enough but because they cared too much to keep participating in something they had come to see as dishonest.

## What the Leavers Still Hunger For

Here is the part of the story that should keep every pastor, every denominational leader, every seminary professor awake at night: the people who left the church did not stop being hungry.

Casper ter Kuile's research at Harvard Divinity School, published in *The Power of Ritual* (2020), documented the ways in which people who have left organized religion are building alternative communities of meaning, purpose, and connection. CrossFit gyms function as covenant communities with shared suffering, mutual accountability, and communal identity. SoulCycle classes use candles, music, and inspirational language that is indistinguishable from a worship service. The Sunday Assembly movement explicitly offers "church for people who don't do God," complete with singing, readings, moments of reflection, and community meals.

These substitutes are revealing. They demonstrate that the needs the church exists to meet, the hunger for community, meaning, transcendence, moral formation, and encounters with something larger than the self, are not going away simply because the church is failing to meet them. Human beings are, as the sociologist Christian Smith has argued, "moral, believing animals." The question is not whether people will seek meaning and belonging. The question is where.

The research consistently identifies four persistent hungers among those who have left the church. The first is community: not the superficial friendliness of a church lobby but genuine, vulnerable, accountable relationships in which people are known and loved in their complexity. The second is meaning: a coherent narrative that makes sense of suffering, injustice, and death, something more robust than "everything happens for a reason" and more honest than "God has a plan." The third is transcendence: encounter with mystery, beauty, and awe, the sense that the universe is not merely material but shot through with significance. The fourth is justice: the conviction that faith should make the world more humane, not less, and that a God worth worshipping is a God who cares about the poor, the marginalized, and the oppressed.

Notice that every one of these hungers is something the church, at its best, is uniquely positioned to address. The church has two millennia of communal practice. It has a story vast enough to encompass every human experience. It has a liturgical tradition designed to cultivate encounters with the sacred. It has a prophetic tradition that has consistently demanded justice for the vulnerable. The raw materials are all there. The failure is not one of resources but of will, honesty, and imagination.

## What the Church Must Hear

The people who have left the church are not its enemies. They are, in many cases, its most honest critics, the ones who loved it enough to be wounded by its failures and clear-eyed enough to name what went wrong. If the church cannot hear their voices without becoming defensive, it will continue to decline, not because the world is hostile to faith but because the institution has become hostile to honesty.

The sociologist Robert Bellah, in *Habits of the Heart* (1985), warned that American individualism was eroding the institutional structures that made community life possible. He was right. But the solution to individualism is not to demand that people return to institutions that have not earned their trust. The solution is to build institutions worthy of trust, communities that tell the truth about their own failures, that welcome questions instead of punishing them, that practice the justice they preach, and that offer not certainty but faithfulness.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison in 1944, anticipated much of what we are witnessing. "We are moving toward a completely religionless time," he wrote. "People as they are now simply cannot be religious anymore." Bonhoeffer did not see this as a catastrophe. He saw it as an invitation, an opportunity for the church to strip away the institutional scaffolding and cultural prestige that had accumulated over centuries and rediscover what was essential: Jesus Christ, present in the midst of human suffering, calling his followers not to power but to service.

Bonhoeffer was executed by the Nazis in April 1945. He never had the chance to develop his vision of a "religionless Christianity." But his intuition was prophetically precise. The institutional trappings that the church clings to most fiercely, the buildings, the budgets, the cultural influence, the political access, are precisely the things that are driving people away. And the thing the church has always claimed to be about, encounter with a God who enters the world's suffering and transforms it from within, is precisely the thing people are still looking for.

> The exodus from the church is not a crisis of faith. It is a crisis of integrity. People are not leaving because they have too little hunger for God. They are leaving because the church has too little hunger for honesty. And until the institution can hear that distinction, the bleeding will not stop.

The question before the church is not how to get people back. That framing already reveals the problem, treating human beings as a resource to be acquired rather than a community to be formed. The question is whether the church is willing to become the kind of community that people would not want to leave: truthful, just, humble, intellectually serious, spiritually alive, and genuinely committed to the way of Jesus rather than the preservation of its own institutional life.

That is a harder question. And the answer, so far, is not encouraging.

chapters.title: Why Young Adults Aren't Coming Back
chapters.summary: The exodus of 18-to-35-year-olds from American churches is not a mystery, and it is not about worship style. It is about credibility, and the church is losing on every front that matters to this generation.
chapters.body:
The numbers are no longer debatable. According to the Pew Research Center's 2021 survey, only 36 percent of Millennials and 31 percent of Generation Z identify as Protestant or Catholic, compared to 67 percent of the Silent Generation. The American Enterprise Institute's 2023 study found that fewer than one in four adults under 30 attends a religious service monthly. Gallup's longitudinal data shows that church membership among Americans aged 18-29 dropped from 51 percent in 1999 to 36 percent in 2020, and that was before the pandemic accelerated the decline. The Survey Center on American Life at AEI reports that roughly 40 percent of Generation Z identifies as religiously unaffiliated, the highest percentage for any generation in American history.

These are not fluctuations. They are not a phase. They represent a structural shift in the relationship between American young adults and organized religion, a shift that shows no signs of reversing. And the church's dominant responses to this crisis reveal, with painful clarity, that most congregations do not understand what is happening to them or why.

The temptation is to frame this as a problem of marketing, as though the church were a product that simply needs better packaging. This instinct is catastrophically wrong, and acting on it has only accelerated the exodus. The young adults who are leaving (or who never arrived) are not looking for a more appealing consumer experience. They are asking whether the church is telling the truth. And too often, they are concluding that it is not.

## What the Church Thinks the Problem Is

Walk into any denominational meeting, any pastoral conference, any megachurch leadership summit where the question of reaching young adults is on the agenda, and you will hear a remarkably consistent set of proposed solutions. Better coffee in the lobby. A more contemporary worship band. Fog machines and LED screens. A "young adult pastor" with skinny jeans and a curated Instagram presence. A sermon series on "relevant" topics, dating, anxiety, career discernment, delivered with self-deprecating humor and pop culture references. A rebrand that removes the word "church" from the name in favor of something that sounds like a boutique coworking space.

These efforts are not merely insufficient. They are actively counterproductive. Every young adult can see exactly what is happening: an institution attempting to disguise itself as something it is not. The effect is not attraction but repulsion. It communicates that the church has so little confidence in its own message that it must borrow credibility from consumer culture. A twenty-five-year-old who grew up marinated in advertising, who has been sold to since before she could read, can detect inauthenticity with the precision of a trained sommelier detecting cork taint. The church's attempts at cultural relevance do not read as relevant. They read as desperate.

The sociological data confirms this. The Barna Group's extensive research on young adult disengagement, published in their 2011 study *You Lost Me* and updated in subsequent surveys, identifies six primary reasons young adults leave the church. Not one of them is "the music was not contemporary enough." Not one is "the coffee was inadequate." The reasons are: the church feels overprotective, shallow, anti-science, repressive, exclusive, and unfriendly to doubt. These are not aesthetic complaints. They are credibility complaints. They concern the substance of what the church teaches and practices, not the style in which it is delivered.

## What Young Adults Actually Want: Authenticity

The word "authenticity" has been so overused in church growth literature that it has nearly lost its meaning. But the concept it points to is real and specific. Young adults are not looking for perfection. They are looking for honesty, including, and especially, honesty about imperfection.

A church that presents itself as having all the answers alienates young adults who live daily with ambiguity, complexity, and uncertainty. A pastor who never admits doubt, never acknowledges the difficulty of a biblical text, never confesses that some questions do not have easy answers, that pastor is not perceived as strong. He is perceived as dishonest. Young adults have watched too many leaders who projected certainty in public and were exposed as frauds in private. The crisis of pastoral credibility, from Ted Haggard to Jerry Falwell Jr. to Ravi Zacharias, has made this generation deeply allergic to performative confidence.

What authenticity looks like in practice is painfully simple and painfully rare. It looks like a pastor saying "I do not know" when confronted with a question that has no clear answer. It looks like a church that acknowledges its own history of complicity in injustice rather than whitewashing its past. It looks like worship that makes space for lament, not just celebration, that takes seriously the reality of suffering rather than papering over it with triumphalist choruses. It looks like a community where vulnerability is modeled from the pulpit, not just expected from the pews.

The churches that are actually reaching young adults understand this intuitively. They tend to be smaller, less polished, and more willing to sit with discomfort. They do not have all the answers, and they are not embarrassed by this. They have traded the performance of certainty for the practice of honest wrestling, and young adults, starved for institutions that do not pretend, find this irresistible.

## The Justice Factor

If authenticity is the doorway, justice is the hallway. For adults under thirty-five, a church's credibility is inseparable from its engagement with systemic injustice, and on this front, the American church has been failing catastrophically for decades.

The data here is unambiguous. The Public Religion Research Institute's 2022 survey found that 70 percent of adults aged 18-29 believe that racism remains a significant problem in American society. Yet when these same young adults look at the church, what do they see? In the aftermath of George Floyd's murder in 2020, the majority of white evangelical churches either said nothing, offered vaguely spiritual platitudes about "unity," or actively opposed the language of systemic racism as a secular ideology incompatible with the gospel. The Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution acknowledging the reality of racism in 2019, only to see prominent leaders spend the next two years arguing that Critical Race Theory was a greater threat to the church than racism itself. For young adults who watched Black men and women die on their phone screens, the church's response was not just inadequate. It was morally disqualifying.

Climate is another front on which the church has surrendered credibility with an entire generation. A 2023 Pew survey found that 76 percent of adults under 30 say climate change is a major threat. Among white evangelicals of all ages, that number drops to 23 percent. Young adults who take seriously the scientific consensus on climate change, which is to say, the overwhelming majority of young adults, encounter a church that either ignores the issue entirely or actively dismisses it as a distraction from "the real gospel." The theological resources for environmental engagement are rich: the creation mandate, the prophetic tradition of caring for the land, the eschatological vision of a renewed earth. That the church has largely refused to deploy these resources in the face of a crisis that defines this generation's future is, for many young adults, evidence that the church cares more about political alignment than about the world God made.

Poverty presents a similar pattern. Young adults facing student debt, stagnant wages, and a housing market that has locked them out of homeownership look to churches and see institutions that preach individual responsibility while ignoring systemic economic structures. The biblical prophets, Amos, Micah, Isaiah, thundered against economic injustice with a specificity that would make most modern pastors profoundly uncomfortable. Yet the average evangelical sermon on poverty amounts to "be generous with your tithe" without engaging the structural questions of why, in the wealthiest nation in history, millions of people cannot afford medical care. For young adults who live these economic realities daily, the church's silence on systemic injustice is not neutral. It is a loud statement about whose interests the church serves.

## The Inclusion Factor

No single issue has driven more young adults from the church than its posture toward LGBTQ+ people. The data on this point is overwhelming and has been consistent for over a decade.

Barna's research has found that the most common perception of the church among non-churchgoing young adults is that it is "anti-homosexual", more common than "judgmental," "hypocritical," or "too political," all of which also rank high. PRRI's 2023 data shows that 79 percent of Americans aged 18-29 support same-sex marriage, including 51 percent of young white evangelicals. The gap between the church's official teaching and the moral convictions of an entire generation is not a gap. It is a chasm.

This is not the place to adjudicate the theological question of same-sex relationships. Faithful Christians hold a range of positions, and the exegetical and hermeneutical arguments are complex. But what must be said, what the church cannot avoid saying if it wants to understand why young adults are leaving, is that the *way* the church has engaged this issue has been, for millions of young adults, the single most powerful evidence that the church is not a safe or credible institution.

Young adults have watched churches use LGBTQ+ people as rhetorical targets while ignoring divorce, materialism, and gossip. They have watched pastors devote sermon after sermon to sexual ethics while remaining silent on racial injustice. They have watched denominations invest millions of dollars in political campaigns against same-sex marriage while cutting budgets for homeless ministries. They have watched families expel their own children in the name of biblical fidelity. The message received, regardless of the message intended, is that the church's moral passion is selective, and that its selectivity correlates suspiciously with the populations it finds most culturally threatening.

For a generation that counts LGBTQ+ people among their closest friends, family members, and colleagues, and that sees no contradiction between this reality and genuine faith, the church's posture is not merely a disagreement. It is a moral emergency. And increasingly, it is a dealbreaker.

## The Hypocrisy Factor

Beneath the specific issues of justice and inclusion lies a deeper problem: the perception, grounded in abundant evidence, that the church does not practice what it preaches.

Young adults watched eighty-one percent of white evangelicals vote for a thrice-married casino owner who bragged about sexual assault, and then heard those same evangelicals lecture them about sexual morality. They watched church leaders who preached "family values" endorse policies that separated migrant children from their parents at the border. They watched pastors who thundered against "the world" accumulate personal wealth that would have scandalized the apostle Paul. They watched denominations that preached the authority of scripture ignore the parts of scripture that addressed their own sins while weaponizing the parts that addressed other people's.

The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his landmark *A Secular Age*, argued that the modern "malaise of immanence", the sense of spiritual flatness that characterizes secular societies, is not primarily the result of intellectual arguments against God but of the failure of religious institutions to embody a compelling alternative to consumer capitalism. Young adults are not, by and large, philosophical materialists. Surveys consistently show that the majority describe themselves as "spiritual" even when they reject organized religion. They have not lost interest in transcendence. They have lost confidence that the church has access to it.

This is the hypocrisy factor at its deepest level. It is not merely that individual Christians are imperfect, every young adult understands that, and most would be drawn to a community that honestly acknowledged its imperfection. The problem is that the church as an institution systematically behaves in ways that contradict its own stated values, and then deploys theological language to justify the contradiction. When a pastor preaches humility from a stage designed to center his own celebrity, the medium contradicts the message. When a church preaches generosity while building a $130 million worship center, the budget contradicts the sermon. When a denomination preaches the authority of scripture while ignoring the 2,000 verses about poverty, the selectivity reveals the real authority: not the text, but the culture that determines which parts of the text to emphasize.

Young adults see this with devastating clarity, and they do not have the institutional loyalty to overlook it.

## The Digital Factor

The pandemic accelerated a trend that was already well underway: the migration of spiritual life from embodied community to digital consumption. By 2021, the Barna Group found that one in three practicing Christians had stopped attending church entirely, with many replacing in-person participation with online content, podcasts, livestreams, YouTube sermons, and the curated social media presence of celebrity pastors.

For young adults, this shift has a particular valence. They have grown up in an ecosystem of parasocial relationships, one-directional connections with media figures who feel intimate but are not. A young adult who listens to a popular pastor's podcast three times a week, follows that pastor on Instagram, and watches their sermon livestream on Sunday may feel genuinely connected to that pastor and that community. But the connection is illusory. There is no mutual knowledge, no shared obligation, no friction, no cost. It is community without covenant, all the emotional resonance of belonging with none of the demands.

This is, in one sense, the ultimate consumer religion: a spiritual experience optimized for individual preference, available on demand, and requiring no sacrifice. It is also profoundly insufficient. The New Testament knows nothing of disembodied faith. The church, in Paul's theology, is a body, not a metaphor for a body, but an actual community of people who bear one another's burdens, confront one another's sins, share one another's meals, and are physically present to one another in suffering. You cannot weep with those who weep through a screen. You cannot bear a burden you do not know about because your only connection to the community is a weekly livestream. You cannot be formed into the image of Christ by a parasocial relationship with a charismatic communicator.

The digital factor is thus both a symptom and a cause of the exodus. It is a symptom because it reveals what young adults find missing in actual churches, they would not seek digital substitutes if the embodied reality were compelling. And it is a cause because the more spiritual life is consumed digitally, the less capacity people develop for the difficult, friction-filled, deeply transformative experience of actual community. The church's competitor is not other churches. It is the entire architecture of digital life, which offers an endless supply of content that feels like connection without any of the cost.

## What Churches That Are Reaching Young Adults Do Differently

Despite the bleak data, there are churches that are reaching young adults, not by chasing cultural trends but by recovering something ancient. These churches share several characteristics that are worth examining closely because they point toward a way forward that does not require the church to abandon its identity.

**They practice radical honesty.** These churches do not pretend to have all the answers. They create space for questions, doubt, and intellectual struggle. They engage seriously with science, philosophy, and the genuine difficulties of biblical interpretation. They do not treat doubt as a spiritual disease to be cured but as a necessary companion to mature faith. The model here is not the certainty of the lecture hall but the honesty of the seminar room, a community of learners wrestling together with texts and traditions that are genuinely difficult.

**They engage justice concretely, not abstractly.** These churches do not merely preach about justice; they practice it. They run legal clinics for undocumented immigrants. They organize tenant unions. They show up at school board meetings. They partner with community organizations that address systemic issues. Their justice engagement is not a program staffed by volunteers; it is embedded in the church's identity and budget. Young adults can tell the difference between a church that talks about justice and a church that spends money on it.

**They demand something.** This may be the most counterintuitive finding: the churches that attract young adults are not the ones that ask the least of them but the ones that ask the most. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's distinction between cheap grace and costly grace is acutely relevant here. A faith that costs nothing is worth nothing, and young adults know it. The churches that are growing among this demographic tend to have rigorous membership processes, high expectations for community participation, and a clear sense of shared mission that requires actual sacrifice. Young adults are not looking for a low-commitment social club. They are looking for something worth giving their lives to.

**They practice genuine community.** Not community as a buzzword in a mission statement, but community as a daily reality, shared meals, mutual aid, physical proximity, honest conflict and honest reconciliation. These churches tend to be smaller, often meeting in homes or shared spaces rather than purpose-built campuses. They emphasize small groups not as a program but as the primary expression of church life. They create structures in which people actually know one another, not as fellow audience members at a weekly performance, but as members of an actual body with actual obligations to one another.

**They separate the faith from partisan politics.** Young adults have watched the church become so entangled with one political party that the gospel itself has become a partisan artifact. Churches that reach young adults tend to be politically engaged but not politically captured. They speak prophetically to both parties. They refuse to let the gospel be reduced to a voter guide. They recover the biblical tradition of prophetic critique that stands outside all human power structures rather than baptizing any one of them.

> "The church that is married to the spirit of this age will be widowed in the next.", William Ralph Inge

The path forward for the American church is not more fog machines. It is not better branding. It is not a hipper pastor or a sleeker app. The path forward is the painful, exhilarating work of becoming what the church claims to be: a community that tells the truth, practices justice, welcomes the stranger, sits with suffering, demands sacrifice, and points beyond itself to a reality that consumer culture cannot provide. Young adults are not leaving the church because they have outgrown the need for transcendence. They are leaving because the church has failed to provide it.

The good news, and it is genuinely good news, is that the solution is not innovation but recovery. Everything the church needs to reach this generation, it already possesses. The prophetic tradition. The practice of radical hospitality. The theology of a God who enters suffering rather than explaining it away. The vision of a community that crosses every boundary the world erects. The church does not need to become something new. It needs to become what it always claimed to be. And if it does, if it trades performance for honesty, comfort for justice, and cultural power for prophetic faithfulness, it will find that the generation it thought it had lost was waiting for it all along.

chapters.title: How to Live as Exiles
chapters.summary: This book has spent nine chapters on why the church lost its power. The subtitle promised the harder thing: how to follow Jesus now that it has. The answer the Bible gives is not retreat and not a fight to take the culture back. It is a word the church forgot it knew. Exile.
chapters.body:
A book that only explains why the church is dying has done half a job and the easier half. The subtitle of this one promised the harder thing, how to actually follow Jesus now that the cultural power is gone, and that requires a word most of us have avoided because it sounds like defeat. The word is exile.

We avoid it because we hear it as surrender. But in Scripture exile is not the end of the story, it is a location God's people have lived in before, faithfully, and even fruitfully, and the Bible is not shy about how. When Judah was hauled off to Babylon, everything that had propped up its faith was gone, the temple, the king, the land, the whole apparatus of a religion that had run the culture. It was the death of a kind of Christendom a thousand years early. And into that loss the prophet Jeremiah sent a letter that is the most surprising instruction in the Old Testament. He did not tell them to fight their way home, and he did not tell them to hunker down and wait it out. He told them to move in. "But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7). Seek the good of Babylon. The city that conquered you. That is the posture, and it is neither the culture war nor the retreat.

The New Testament simply assumes this is now the church's permanent address. Peter opens his letter to Christians scattered across a hostile empire by calling them "elect exiles" (1 Peter 1:1), and later, "sojourners and exiles" (1 Peter 2:11). Not exiles as a complaint. Exiles as an identity, and a strategy. These were people with no political power, no cultural prestige, no path to taking the empire back, and Peter does not spend a word wishing they had those things. He tells them to live such good lives among the pagans that the accusations fall apart, to honor the emperor who may kill them, to be ready to give a reason for their hope with gentleness and respect. That is a playbook for a church that has lost, and it is the playbook that won.

Because here is the thing the death of Christendom lets us finally admit. The church was rarely at its best when it ran things. The centuries when it held the sword and the throne are not the centuries of its purest witness, they are the centuries of its worst compromises, the crusade and the inquisition and the state church that persecuted dissenters and blessed whatever the king wanted blessed. Cultural power was never the church's friend. It was a slow bribe. And it is at least possible that losing it is not only a judgment but a mercy, God prying loose a grip that was corrupting us, handing us back the one posture in which the church has always been most itself, which is the posture of the powerless who have nothing to defend but the truth and nothing to offer but love.

So what does following Jesus look like on the far side of Christendom? It looks like Daniel, serving Babylon with excellence and refusing, at the cost of his life, to bow. It looks like the early church, a tiny minority that took in the babies Rome threw away and nursed the plague victims everyone else fled, until an empire that despised them could not explain them. It looks like what one sociologist has called faithful presence, neither storming the culture nor hiding from it, but staying, deeply and locally, being the kind of neighbor and church and family that makes the watching world wonder what you know that it does not. It looks like recovering the ordinary means we let slip when we thought the culture would do our discipleship for us, teaching the faith to our own children as if no one else will, gathering to worship as if it is the most important thing we do, practicing a hospitality the anxious world has forgotten how to give.

None of that requires the church to be in charge. All of it requires the church to be faithful, which is the only thing it was ever actually asked to be. The exiles in Babylon did not get their nation back on their timeline. They got seventy years, and a God who was with them in the fire, and a faith that came out of exile deeper and truer than the comfortable religion that went in. That is the offer on the table for a church at the end of Christendom. Not the restoration of a power we should be relieved to lose. Something better. The chance to follow Jesus for his own sake again, in a land that is not our home, on the way to a city that is.
